Harness Engineering, day one: what happened when my new AI employee got his first task on my motion workflow.

The job was motion -> studio, my instruction package for making a product film with Opus 5.5. Files existed, the promo was already rendered. The weak spot was the handoff - which prompt does a reader open first, and do they really get every file the README mentions?

That kind of checking is part of shipping, and it's a perfect task for a new hire. So I dropped it on viktor in our studio Slack and asked him to inspect the package and write reader guidance.

He returned four documents and flagged seven referenced records that never made it into the transfer.

Turns out the mistake was mine. The records lived in my project - I just never included them.

Below: the task, what his first pass caught, my correction, his revision, the note I signed off and the final result.

How to Write a CLAUDE.md for Your Obsidian Vault ( Full Course)

Most people point Claude Code at their Obsidian vault and type "organize my notes."
Then they wonder why it renamed 200 files, rewrote their journal and invented a folder structure nobody asked for.
Claude didn't fail.
It just had no idea how YOUR brain is organized.
The fix is one file.
CLAUDE.md.
It sits in the root of your vault, Claude Code reads it automatically every time it starts, and it turns a brilliant stranger into an assistant who already knows how you think.
This course shows you exactly how to write one. From scratch. Section by section. With templates for writers, founders, students and researchers.
By the end you'll have:
A CLAUDE.md that makes Claude behave the same way every session
Rules that protect your notes from ever being damaged
Folder level instructions for different parts of your vault
A way to test it, fix it and keep it short
Bookmark this. You'll come back to it.
Module 1: What CLAUDE.md actually does
When you start Claude Code inside a folder, it looks for a file called CLAUDE.md and loads it into its context before you say anything.
That means every instruction in that file shapes every answer in that session.

Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.

I’ve been a ChatGPT Pro subscriber for a long time and have used ChatGPT since GPT-3.5.

GPT Instant is delightful, especially for learning, and the new intelligent UI makes it even better. Codex and ChatGPT Desktop desperately need this experience.

Right now, Codex models feel like research and engineering machines. Claude models feel like educators, tutors, artists, and experienced human engineers.

Codex is competent, but its communication and design instincts are frustrating:

Explaining: Excessive negation, caveats, and self-clarification make simple concepts confusing.
Designing: Too much helper text, taglines, descriptions, and unnecessary UI clutter.

I suspect this is partly a consequence of the GPT-4o sycophancy controversy. The models became highly capable but lost some of their natural, human-like qualities.

I’m not advocating Anthropic’s nonsense about model consciousness or policing how users speak to AI. I’m asking for models that are excellent at both engineering and teaching.

My suggestion: Bring GPT Instant and its intelligent UI seamlessly into ChatGPT Desktop/Codex, or build a Codex model that’s genuinely excellent at teaching, explaining, and design.

That would be a huge win. @thsottiaux @sama

outsiders.text:
Every added layer of complexity in an application makes it 10x harder to describe and make content on. 

Back in April I was making many videos on Codex. 

"Codex, OpenAI's version of Claude Code" 
"Codex, the desktop app on your computer"
"Codex, the super app that can do any CPU task"

Very, very easy to describe. 
Repeatable, and viral. 

This made it effortless to describe on short form or long from videos.

Then ChatGPT and Codex merged. 

Okay, now Codex is not an app. 
Codex is a feature inside ChatGPT. 

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT Desktop app"

Okay, now ChatGPT has "GPT Work"

"Codex, the AI coding agent feature inside the ChatGPT desktop app that allows you to do coding tasks, and sometimes work tasks, some of those should be done inside GPT Work, which is kind of similar, but like different, depending on if you are using Cloud GPT Work, or local GPT work, in which case is alot closer to Codex, but still not quite the same. If you try and use the skills you created on Codex they won't work when doing a cloud GPT Work session but if it's a local session it will work."

We haven't even made it to Codex Cloud sessions, GPT Dots, and GPT Plugins yet. 

This goes for anyone building software. If you want to create an ecosystem of creators who talk about your product organically, you should aim for simplicity.

BTW not saying it was the wrong decision for OpenAI to merge them, i'm just saying for me it got much harder to describe with every new feature added.

I’ve been a ChatGPT Pro subscriber for a long time and have used ChatGPT since GPT-3.5.

GPT Instant is delightful, especially for learning, and the new intelligent UI makes it even better. Codex and ChatGPT Desktop desperately need this experience.

Right now, Codex models feel like research and engineering machines. Claude models feel like educators, tutors, artists, and experienced human engineers.

Codex is competent, but its communication and design instincts are frustrating:

Explaining: Excessive negation, caveats, and self-clarification make simple concepts confusing.
Designing: Too much helper text, taglines, descriptions, and unnecessary UI clutter.

I suspect this is partly a consequence of the GPT-4o sycophancy controversy. The models became highly capable but lost some of their natural, human-like qualities.

I’m not advocating Anthropic’s nonsense about model consciousness or policing how users speak to AI. I’m asking for models that are excellent at both engineering and teaching.

My suggestion: Bring GPT Instant and its intelligent UI seamlessly into ChatGPT Desktop/Codex, or build a Codex model that’s genuinely excellent at teaching, explaining, and design.

That would be a huge win. @thsottiaux @sama
